speaker: Rory Sutherland
title: Marketing Expert: The Playbook Behind Every Great Campaign | Rory Sutherland
question: In consumer product design, why do single-option AI recommendations often fail to convert buyers even when the recommendation is objectively strong?
guest: I keep hearing people saying, "You will say to your AI, find me a skiing holiday, and it will provide you with the perfect skiing holiday." And I keep saying, "People don't decide like that." At the very least, you'll have to show them three or four or five skiing holidays from which they choose, because we can't really choose in the absence of comparison. We can only like something if we choose it in preference to something else. Among real estate agents, there's a trick: before you show someone the house you want to sell them, you show them a less appropriate house, ideally slightly more expensive, so that when they see the house you want to sell them, it's clear-cut because they can say, "Oh, it's cheaper than the other one, and it's got a conservatory." So there's a decoy effect. Nobody clicks the "I'm Feeling Lucky" button on Google—the number of people who click "take me straight to a single page" is vanishingly small. People want to choose between above-the-fold options. It's very easy for people with an economic or tech background to assume we're utility maximizers, only to be completely wrong.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Single-option recommendations tend to fail because buyers need to feel they made a choice, not that one was made for them. Several well-documented effects are at work.

The first is single-option aversion: research by Daniel Mochon found that people shown only one attractive product are less likely to buy it than when it appears alongside alternatives, and instead keep searching. Without a comparison, they cannot judge whether the option is good, so "objectively strong" has no visible reference point.

The second is autonomy. A lone recommendation can feel like a push, triggering reactance and suspicion about whose interests the system serves, especially when the reasoning is opaque. Algorithm aversion compounds this, since people discount AI advice more readily than human advice, particularly for subjective or personal purchases.

The third is justification. Buyers want to explain their decision to themselves and others, and "it beat these alternatives on what I care about" is far more persuasive than "the AI said so."

The usual design fix is a small, curated set of two to four options with a highlighted top pick, a short explanation of why it fits, and visible trade-offs.

models.answer:
Single-option AI recommendations often fail because people judge value comparatively rather than in isolation, a behavioral effect known as single-option aversion. Without alternatives to anchor price, features, and trade-offs, buyers lack the reference points needed to verify why an objectively strong product is worthwhile. Instead of purchasing, they defer the decision and search elsewhere to confirm nothing better exists.

AI interfaces compound this hesitation through opacity and reduced agency. When a black-box system outputs one definitive answer without showing runner-up contenders, shoppers cannot inspect what was filtered out and frequently suspect commercial bias, sponsored placement, or misunderstood preferences. Receiving a lone prescription also triggers psychological reactance: turning an active chooser into a passive recipient threatens perceived autonomy, especially when tastes are subjective or financial stakes are high.

Offering two or three contrasting options resolves these barriers simultaneously, making trade-offs legible, exposing the AI’s selection logic, and preserving the final agency buyers need to commit with confidence.

noweb.answer:
Single-option AI recommendations often fail because they trigger single-option aversion and strip away the comparative context buyers need to feel confident. Humans evaluate value relatively rather than in isolation; without reference points for price, features, and trade-offs, even an objectively optimal product is difficult to judge. Presenting just one item shifts the shopper's mental frame from choosing among finalists to deciding whether to buy now or keep searching, frequently driving them elsewhere to validate the pick on their own.

Furthermore, a solitary recommendation undermines perceived autonomy and invites algorithmic distrust. When an opaque system dictates a single answer, buyers often experience psychological reactance or suspect the platform is pushing high-margin inventory rather than serving their genuine interests. Offering two or three curated alternatives resolves these tensions simultaneously: contrasting options make trade-offs legible, anchor the value of the leading recommendation, and restore the buyer's sense of agency, turning passive skepticism into an informed, confident purchase.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Single-option recommendations often fail because people judge value by comparing options, not by looking at one option alone. Daniel Mochon's research on "single-option aversion" (2013) found that consumers offered just one product are more likely to put off buying, even when it's a good product. When a competing option is added, purchases go up, even if the new option is no better. Without anything to compare against, a buyer can't tell whether the pick is actually good. So they keep searching, and often they leave.

A lone recommendation can also feel like the system is choosing for the buyer, which triggers reactance, the urge to push back against a threat to one's own control. People want to feel they decided. That loss of control adds to algorithm aversion: they distrust an opaque system and don't know whose interests it serves.

Committing to one option also makes regret feel personal: "I just took what the AI said." Comparing alternatives gives buyers a reason they can explain to themselves, and that confidence makes them more willing to buy.

The usual fix is to show a top pick next to one or two alternatives, explain the trade-offs, and leave the final choice to the buyer.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Even when an AI identifies an objectively strong product, presenting it as a single option triggers single-option aversion: buyers struggle to evaluate an item's quality or value in isolation without a reference point for comparison. Rather than feeling relieved by the shortcut, shoppers often defer the purchase and leave to search elsewhere so they can verify they are not missing a better deal or overlooking important trade-offs.

A lone recommendation also undermines perceived agency. People want to feel that a purchase reflects their own judgment, not an algorithm's decree, and a black-box pick can spark skepticism about whether the system is optimizing for the buyer's needs or the retailer's margins. Offering a small, curated set of alternatives solves both problems by providing clear context for trade-offs, restoring a sense of control, and giving buyers the confidence they need to justify the decision and convert.

A single AI recommendation can be a great match and still leave the buyer wondering, “How do I know this is the right one?” Buyers often need a point of comparison to judge value, understand trade-offs, and feel confident committing. With only one option, the decision becomes “buy this or keep looking,” and continuing to search can feel safer.

This is known as *single-option aversion*. AI can amplify it when shoppers can’t see why the system picked that product or whether it understood what mattered to them. A top pick alongside one or two meaningful alternatives gives buyers a way to check the recommendation against their own priorities. For example, seeing what they’d give up with a cheaper model can make the top pick easier to justify.
